Raven (Doctrine)
RAY-vun
n.
Old English hræfn; Hebrew ‘orēb (raven); Greek korax (raven). The first bird sent forth from Noah’s ark, the bird that fed Elijah at the brook Cherith, and one of Christ’s examples of God’s providential care.

📖 Biblical Definition

The raven is a large black bird (the common raven, Corvus corax) found across the ancient Near East, appearing in three significant biblical contexts that together carry substantial pastoral substance. First, Noah’s raven. Genesis 8:7: when Noah opened the window of the ark and sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth. The raven, unlike the dove that followed it, did not return to the ark—perhaps because the carrion of the post-flood world provided sufficient food and habitation for the unclean bird (the raven was classified as unclean under the Levitical law, Lev 11:15; Deut 14:14, suiting its scavenger habits). The contrast with Noah’s dove is theologically significant: the unclean raven found rest in the death-littered post-flood landscape; the clean dove found no rest until she returned with the olive-leaf sign of new creation. Second, the ravens that fed Elijah at the brook Cherith (1 Kings 17:1-6). When Elijah pronounced the long famine on Ahab’s wicked reign, the LORD directed him to hide by the brook Cherith east of the Jordan: and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there. So he went and did according unto the word of the LORD: for he went and dwelt by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan. And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook. The narrative is one of the most striking providential-care episodes in the OT: God uses ceremonially-unclean birds (ravens were unclean, but the LORD used them as instruments of His provision) to sustain His prophet through the famine. Several pastoral lessons follow. The LORD uses the means He chooses, including unlikely or unclean ones; the prophet’s sustenance comes through unexpected channels at the LORD’s appointment; the same LORD who appoints famine appoints provision through it; the saint may be reduced to the most marginal circumstances and yet be sustained by the LORD’s deliberate provision. Third, Christ’s explicit use of ravens as evidence of God’s providence (Luke 12:24): consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls? Christ chooses the raven specifically—the ceremonially-unclean bird, not the more obviously-favored sparrow or dove—as the example of God’s care, intensifying the argument: if God feeds even the unclean raven that neither sows nor reaps, how much more will He care for His own children? The raven’s presence in Christ’s providence-teaching is therefore not incidental: the unclean bird, the scavenger, the OT-classified-unclean creature is named as the LORD’s provident object precisely to push the argument as far as it will go. The biblical raven-doctrine therefore carries a remarkable range: the unclean bird of Noah’s narrative that suits the post-flood death-landscape; the LORD’s unlikely instrument of provision for Elijah; the unclean bird Christ chooses as His providence-teaching example. The cumulative substance is that the LORD’s providence extends to and uses the unclean, the unlikely, the marginal—and the saint is therefore secure in His care under every circumstance.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines RAVEN as a large bird of the order Picae, of the genus Corvus, black with violet reflections; in scripture, Noah’s first-sent bird that did not return (Gen 8:7), the LORD’s instrument of provision for Elijah at Cherith (1 Kgs 17:6), and Christ’s providence-teaching example (Luke 12:24)—the ceremonially-unclean bird the LORD uses and cares for, pushing the argument from least-likely to greatest.

RAVEN, n. — A large bird of the order Picae, of the genus Corvus, black with violet reflections; an omnivorous scavenger. In scripture, classified as unclean (Lev 11:15), and yet used by the LORD as His instrument of provision for Elijah (1 Kgs 17:6) and as Christ’s providence-teaching example (Luke 12:24).

CHERITH, n. — The brook east of the Jordan to which Elijah was directed, where the ravens brought him bread and flesh morning and evening during the great famine (1 Kgs 17:3-6).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Kings 17:6 — "And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook."

Genesis 8:7 — "And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth."

Luke 12:24 — "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls?"

Job 38:41 — "Who provideth for the raven his food? when his young ones cry unto God, they wander for lack of meat."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The raven-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by being skipped past as obscure bird-detail in much contemporary preaching—missing the substantive providence-and-unlikely-instruments teaching that the cumulative biblical raven-references carry, especially the LORD’s use of ceremonially-unclean ravens to sustain Elijah and Christ’s deliberate choice of the unclean raven as His providence-example.

expand to see more

Contemporary preaching often skips the biblical-bird references entirely, treating them as quaint zoological detail without operative theological substance. The cumulative raven-references in particular carry teaching the Christian needs. Elijah at Cherith fed by ravens illustrates the LORD’s use of unlikely instruments for the sustenance of His servants: the prophet whose preaching had brought him into hiding is fed by ceremonially-unclean birds at the LORD’s direct appointment. The lesson is direct: the LORD’s provision comes through whatever means He chooses, including means the prophet would never have imagined or selected; the saint reduced to marginal circumstances need not despair, because the same LORD who appoints the famine appoints provision through it. Christ’s use of the raven in Luke 12:24 amplifies the argument: if God feeds even the unclean raven, how much more will He care for His own children? The recovery is the recovery of these substantive providence-teaching passages, which the cumulative raven-references gather into a coherent biblical pastoral substance.

The deeper pattern is the LORD’s deliberate use of the unclean, the unlikely, and the marginal as instruments of His care—a pattern that runs across many biblical narratives but that the raven-references particularly anchor. Christ’s choice of the raven for His providence-teaching is not incidental but rhetorically strategic: the unclean bird that neither sows nor reaps is the example that pushes the argument as far as it will go. If God’s providence extends to the unclean raven, the LORD’s care for His own children must be incomparably greater. The contemporary believer who fears providential abandonment, who feels marginal or unworthy of God’s care, who imagines that his circumstances have placed him outside the LORD’s notice, is to consider the raven: the unclean bird that the LORD feeds, the scavenger that the LORD provides for, the OT-classified-unclean creature that Christ deliberately named in His providence-teaching. The argument is: if God’s care extends so far, then it certainly extends to His own children. Recover the raven-doctrine, and the saint recovers also the deep providential confidence the biblical pattern is meant to produce.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ‘orēb (raven) and Greek korax (raven); the OT unclean bird (Lev 11:15) used by the LORD as His instrument of providence for Elijah (1 Kgs 17:6) and chosen by Christ as the providence-teaching example (Luke 12:24) precisely because its uncleanness pushes the argument as far as it will go: if God feeds even the raven, how much more will He care for His own children.

Hebrew ‘orēb (H6158) — raven (11 OT uses).

Greek korax (G2876) — raven (Luke 12:24, the singular NT use).

Hebrew tamē’ — unclean (the Levitical classification of the raven; Lev 11:15; Deut 14:14).

Hebrew Cherīth (H3747) — Cherith (the brook east of the Jordan where the ravens fed Elijah, 1 Kgs 17:3-6).
